title: How Attila the Hun Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck (with guest producer Dylan) profile Attila the Hun: the uncertainty about his early life and language, the Huns as nomadic horse-archers known for pillage and terror tactics (the "scourge of God" name), his co-rule with brother Bleda and Bleda's murder, his simple lifestyle, the Treaty of Margus and extortion of gold from the Eastern Roman Empire, the domino effect of tribes pushed into Rome (Great Migration), the Honoria engagement-ring episode that prompted an invasion of the Western Empire, his marriage to Ildico and death from a nosebleed/burst artery on the wedding night, his one defeat in Gaul, and his supposed secret burial in a diverted river in three coffins. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about lamplighters (a Spanish folk song and tips to lamplighters) and a request about how CAPTCHA works, then sign-off.
topics: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and comparing Attila with Genghis Khan
segments.summary: Hosts joke about guest producer Dylan, then compare Attila the Hun with Genghis Khan, noting the roughly thousand-year gap, uncertainty about Attila's early life and language, and the Huns as barbarian nomads who pillaged rather than ruled.

segments.title: Attila's birth and Hun warfare
segments.summary: Attila is thought to have been born around 406 in Pannonia (modern Hungary). The hosts describe the Huns as expert horsemen who fought from horseback, used the short recurve Hun bow, wore greased leather and chain mail, and attacked without formation.

segments.title: Hun raids, Aquileia, and the Scourge of God
segments.summary: The hosts describe how Huns levelled towns such as Aquileia, how Attila used his fearsome reputation to induce surrender, and the name Flagellum Dei, the Scourge of God, given by Christians who saw the attacks as divine punishment; historians doubt Attila coined it.

segments.title: Co-rule with Bleda and Attila's rise
segments.summary: Attila and his brother Bleda ruled jointly after their uncles, becoming co-rulers in 434. Attila later killed Bleda to rule alone. The name Attila is said to mean 'little father' and was likely a title of respect. Attila was educated in Latin and statecraft.

segments.title: Attila's simple lifestyle and the Treaty of Margus
segments.summary: Attila lived simply in a log house and drank from wooden cups while his subordinates lived lavishly. In 434 the Treaty of Margus required Rome to return Hun refugees and pay about 700 pounds of gold a year. Attila later invaded after a bishop who had stolen grave goods was not handed over, and Rome paid triple tribute.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before continuing.

segments.title: Domino effect and fall of Rome
segments.summary: Hun pressure pushed Alans, Goths and other Germanic tribes into the Roman Empire, setting off the Great Migration (wandering of the nations). Their conflicts with Rome weakened the empire, and the Goths eventually sacked Rome.
topics: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

segments.title: Honoria's ring and Attila's marriage and death
segments.summary: Honoria, sister of Valentinian III, sent her engagement ring to Attila to avoid an unwanted marriage. Attila treated it as a proposal, demanded half the Western Empire as dowry, and invaded. He also took a wife, Ildico, and died on their wedding night, likely from a nosebleed or burst artery and choking on blood, though assassination was an alternative theory.

segments.title: Battle in Gaul, burial legend, and extra Hun facts
segments.summary: Attila's one notable defeat, a bloody draw in Gaul against Romans and Goths. His followers reportedly buried him in three coffins in a diverted river, a legend paralleled by Gilgamesh and Theodoric I. The hosts also note Huns ate raw meat tenderized under their saddles.

segments.title: Listener mail on lamplighters and CAPTCHA
segments.summary: A listener from Mexico describes couples bribing lamplighters to leave lamps off, and another asks how CAPTCHA works. The hosts sign off.
